zone: Snoqualmie Pass — Chair Peak, The Tooth, Guye Peak

sites.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
sites.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites
sites.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
sites.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.

sites.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
sites.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends
sites.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
sites.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.

sites.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
sites.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack
sites.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
sites.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
sites.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.

sites.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
sites.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site
sites.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
sites.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
sites.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.

sites.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
sites.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites
sites.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
sites.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
sites.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. No elevation is recorded here because a confident figure could not be sourced; it sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
